question:
How can I convert a TypeVarTuple to a ParamSpec?

(I am almost certain the wording of the question does not make sense, but I have yet to find a better one.) I have the following code that I want to type-check: from collections.abc import Callable from typing import Generic, TypeVar, TypeVarTuple C = TypeVar("C") T = TypeVar("T") Ts = TypeVarTuple("Ts") class Decorator1(Generic[T]): def __init__(self, /, type: type[T]) -> None: super().__init__() def __call__(self, function: Callable[[C, T], None], /) -> Callable[[C, T], None]: return function class DecoratorNa(Generic[T]): # Q: how to prevent "T" from becoming "object" here? def __init__(self, /, *type: type[T]) -> None: super().__init__() def __call__(self, function: Callable[[C, T], None], /) -> Callable[[C, T], None]: return function class DecoratorNb(Generic[*Ts]): def __init__(self, /, *types: *Ts) -> None: super().__init__() # Q: how to convert "*Ts" from "type[int], type[str]" to "int, str" here? def __call__( self, function: Callable[[C, *Ts], None], / ) -> Callable[[C, *Ts], None]: return function class MyClass: # This is given and supposed to type-check: @Decorator1(int) def print_number(self, number: int) -> None: ... @Decorator1(str) def print_string(self, string: str) -> None: ... # # This is supposed to error: # @Decorator1(int) # def print_another_string(self, string: str) -> None: ... # This is supposed to type-check: @DecoratorNa(int, str) def print_number_and_string_a(self, number: int, string: str) -> None: ... # This is supposed to type-check: @DecoratorNb(int, str) def print_number_and_string_b(self, number: int, string: str) -> None: ... The construc
reference_answer: As mentioned in the comments, the exact syntax you're using doesn't currently work. Type forms, which allow type-checkers to make sense of call expressions which accept types ( DecoratorNa(int, str) ) are currently being submitted and are in the final stages of revision 1 , but as of today, there is nothing concrete for TypeVarTuple transformation. However, if you're willing to switch syntax from a __call__ ( DecoratorNa(int, str) ) to a __getitem__ ( DecoratorN[int, str] ) expression, the following may work for you ( mypy Playground , Pyright Playground ): ... from types import MethodType ... class DecoratorN(Generic[*Ts]): def __init__( self, function: Callable[[Any, *Ts], None], / ) -> None: super().__init__() self._function = function def __get__(self, instance: Any, owner: type[Any], /) -> Callable[[*Ts], None]: return MethodType(self._function, instance) # type: ignore[return-value] class MyClass: # This is given and supposed to type-check: @Decorator1[int] def print_number(self, number: int) -> None: ... @Decorator1[str] def print_string(self, string: str) -> None: ... @Decorator1[int] # error def print_another_string(self, string: str) -> None: ... @DecoratorN[int, str] def print_number_and_string(self, number: int, string: str) -> None: ... mc: MyClass = MyClass() mc.print_number(1) mc.print_number("") # error mc.print_string("") mc.print_string(1) # error mc.print_number_and_string(1, "") mc.print_number_and_string("", 1) # error Here, the square brackets allow proper interpretation as type parameterisation on the DecoratorN[*Ts] type, which is then used to enforc
llm_attempt:
The title's ParamSpec framing doesn't really match the code; the real issues are TypeVarTuple vs a plain TypeVar. In DecoratorNa, `*type: type[T]` reuses one scalar TypeVar across several positional args. A single TypeVar must resolve to one type consistent with every argument, so int and str can only unify to their join, object. You can't prevent that with a plain TypeVar - you need PEP 646's TypeVarTuple, which is what DecoratorNb correctly does, to bind a distinct type per argument.

For DecoratorNb, `*types: *Ts` means each element of types is a value whose type matches the corresponding Ts slot. Calling DecoratorNb(int, str) passes the class objects int and str, so Ts is inferred as (type[int], type[str]) - the runtime type of each argument - not (int, str). Current Python typing has no operator that strips type[] element-wise across an unpacked TypeVarTuple; there's no mapped-tuple-type feature yet. For small fixed arities, per-arity @overload (as in Decorator1) is still the only checker-supported workaround.

question:
Polars import from list of list into Colums

I am trying to import a list of lists into Polars and get the data in seperate columns. Example. numbers = [['304-144635', 0], ['123-091523', 7], ['305-144931', 12], ['623-101523', 16], ['305-145001', 22], ['623-111523', 27], ['9998-2603', 29]] Does not work like Pandas and this does not work. df = pl.DataFrame(numbers) new to polars and excited to start using. Thanks
reference_answer: You can do pl.DataFrame(numbers, orient="row") if you are okay with the default column names Polars gives you (column_0, column_1). Or (as you show), you can specify the schema if you want to control the names of the columns or their types. Also note that the default column names in Polars are different to those in pandas.
llm_attempt:
Polars needs to know whether each inner list is a row or a column; from a plain list of lists it can guess wrong, especially when row length (2) differs from the number of sublists (7), so it may build columns instead of rows. Pass orient explicitly, and ideally a schema for column names:

df = pl.DataFrame(numbers, schema=["id", "value"], orient="row")

That forces each inner list to become one row with two columns. If you don't set orient and Polars infers the wrong orientation, you'll get 7 columns of length 2 instead of 2 columns of length 7. You can also build it from separate lists for explicit control:

df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [r[0] for r in numbers], "value": [r[1] for r in numbers]})

Either approach avoids the ambiguity that pl.DataFrame(numbers) alone runs into, unlike pandas.DataFrame(numbers), which always treats the outer list as rows.

question:
How can I find the maximum value of a dynamic window and the minimum value below it?

This is my DataFrame: import pandas as pd df = pd.DataFrame( { 'a': [3, 1, 2, 5, 10, 3, 13, 3, 2], } ) Expected output is creating a a_max and a_min : a a_max a_min 0 3 NaN NaN 1 1 3 1 2 2 3 1 3 5 3 1 4 10 3 1 5 3 10 3 6 13 10 3 7 3 13 3 8 2 13 2 Logic: I explain the logic row by row. There is a dynamic window for this df that for the first instance of the window only the first row is considered. For the second instance of the window the first two rows are considered. Same as below: These are the first four windows. It expands accordingly. For each window I need to find the maximum value and after that I need to find the minimum value BELOW that maximum value. I start explaining it from the yellow window. For this window the max value is 3 and the min value BELOW it is 1. So that is why a_max and a_min for this window is 3 and 1. Now for the orange window the maximum value is 5 but since there are no values in this window BELOW this value that is less than 5, the previous a_max and a_min are repeated. And the logic continues for the rest of rows. This is my attempt: df['a_max'] = df.a.cummax() df['a_min'] = df.a.cummin()
reference_answer: This is a tricky one, I would use a cummax + shift , then mask + ffill to compute a_max . Then a_min is the groupby.cummin per group of identical a_max : # compute the shifted cummax cm = df['a'].cummax().shift() # a_max is the cummax except if the current row is larger df['a_max'] = cm.mask(df['a'].gt(cm)).ffill() # a_min is the cummin of the current group of a_max df['a_min'] = df.groupby('a_max')['a'].cummin() Output: a a_max a_min 0 3 NaN NaN 1 1 3.0 1.0 2 2 3.0 1.0 3 5 3.0 1.0 4 10 3.0 1.0 5 3 10.0 3.0 6 13 10.0 3.0 7 3 13.0 3.0 8 2 13.0 2.0 Intermediates: a a_max cummax shift mask ffill a_min 0 3 NaN 3 NaN NaN NaN NaN 1 1 3.0 3 3.0 3.0 3.0 1.0 2 2 3.0 3 3.0 3.0 3.0 1.0 3 5 3.0 5 3.0 NaN 3.0 1.0 4 10 3.0 10 5.0 NaN 3.0 1.0 5 3 10.0 10 10.0 10.0 10.0 3.0 6 13 10.0 13 10.0 NaN 10.0 3.0 7 3 13.0 13 13.0 13.0 13.0 3.0 8 2 13.0 13 13.0 13.0 13.0 2.0
llm_attempt:
This isn't a plain rolling/expanding op - it's stateful and needs a loop. Track running_max and running_min (the min seen since running_max last changed). Whenever the current value exceeds running_max, a new max just started: output stays equal to the previous row's output (nothing below the new max yet), then update running_max and reset running_min. Otherwise, update running_min with the current value and output the current running_max/running_min.

import numpy as np
a = df['a'].to_numpy()
n = len(a)
a_max = np.full(n, np.nan)
a_min = np.full(n, np.nan)
running_max, running_min = a[0], np.nan
for i in range(1, n):
    if a[i] > running_max:
        running_max = a[i]
        running_min = np.nan
        a_max[i], a_min[i] = a_max[i-1], a_min[i-1]
    else:
        running_min = a[i] if np.isnan(running_min) else min(running_min, a[i])
        a_max[i], a_min[i] = running_max, running_min
df['a_max'], df['a_min'] = a_max, a_min

This reproduces your expected table; cummax/cummin alone can't, since they don't freeze output when a fresh max has no data below it yet.

question:
Change placeholder based on latest chat input streamlit

I have this code that supposed to change placeholder dynamically based on latest user input: def main(): last_prompt = st.session_state.get( "last_prompt", "A cat detective interrogating a suspicious goldfish in a bubble-filled aquarium courtroom.") prompt_input = st.chat_input(last_prompt) if prompt_input: st.session_state.last_prompt = prompt_input But it's not working as I expected, the placeholder still show default placeholder instead of latest chat input.
reference_answer: Using st.rerun solved my problem, but I don't know whether this will be performance issue since I heard there is fragmenting mechanism scope. def main(): last_prompt = st.session_state.get( "last_prompt", "A cat detective interrogating a suspicious goldfish in a bubble-filled aquarium courtroom.") prompt_input = st.chat_input(last_prompt) if prompt_input: if prompt_input != st.session_state.last_prompt: st.session_state.last_prompt = prompt_input st.rerun() # rest of my code...
llm_attempt:
st.chat_input's placeholder is only used when the widget is first created on the frontend; on reruns, the chat input component doesn't reliably re-render a changed placeholder prop for what it treats as the "same" widget, so passing a new string each run often has no visible effect - this is a known limitation, not a bug in your logic. Your state-update logic itself is fine: since Streamlit reruns top-to-bottom, session_state.last_prompt set at the bottom of one run is correctly available at the top of the next.

Workaround: force the widget to remount by giving it an explicit key that changes whenever last_prompt changes, e.g. key=f"chat_{hash(last_prompt)}", or keep a counter in session_state that increments on each submission and include it in the key. Also confirm main() is actually being invoked (e.g. at the module bottom: if __name__ == '__main__': main()), since a defined-but-uncalled main() would show the hardcoded default forever regardless of the placeholder logic.

question:
Conditionally slice a pandas multiindex on specific level

For my given multi-indexed DataFrame: df = pd.DataFrame( np.random.randn(12), index=[ [1,1,2,3,4,4,5,5,6,6,7,8], [1,2,1,1,1,2,1,2,1,2,2,2], ] ) 0 1 1 1.667692 2 0.274428 2 1 0.216911 3 1 -0.513463 4 1 -0.642277 2 -2.563876 5 1 2.301943 2 1.455494 6 1 -1.539390 2 -1.344079 7 2 0.300735 8 2 0.089269 I would like to slice it such that I keep only rows where second index level contains BOTH 1 and 2 0 1 1 1.667692 2 0.274428 4 1 -0.642277 2 -2.563876 5 1 2.301943 2 1.455494 6 1 -1.539390 2 -1.344079 How can I do this?
reference_answer: Another possible solution, which is based on the following: df.groupby(level=0) groups the dataframe by the first level of the index. filter(lambda x: set(x.index.get_level_values(1)) == {1, 2}) checks if the second level of the index for each group contains both 1 and 2, and retains only the groups that meet this condition. df.groupby(level=0).filter(lambda x: set(x.index.get_level_values(1)) == {1, 2}) Output: 0 1 1 -1.085631 2 0.997345 4 1 -0.578600 2 1.651437 5 1 -2.426679 2 -0.428913 6 1 1.265936 2 -0.866740
llm_attempt:
Use groupby on level 0 and filter groups whose level-1 values are a superset of {1, 2}:

df.groupby(level=0, group_keys=False).filter(
    lambda g: {1, 2}.issubset(g.index.get_level_values(1))
)

filter() runs your predicate on each group's sub-DataFrame and keeps only the rows belonging to groups where it returns True - no manual index building needed, and it works regardless of how many level-1 values each group has. If you need this repeatedly on a large frame, precomputing the valid level-0 labels once and reusing a boolean mask via get_level_values(0).isin(...) will be faster than re-running filter each time.

question:

Despite I've already tried some of the workarounds that I found on Stack Overflow, I'm still not able to install TA-Lib in my conda enviroment. It seems that a more recent Python version is required, notwithstanding that my Python version is already the most recent. Please see below. (base) C:\Users\salva>conda activate UUSeRR (UUSeRR) C:\Users\salva>mamba install TA-lib Looking for: ['ta-lib'] conda-forge/win-64 Using cache conda-forge/noarch Using cache warning libmamba Could not parse mod/etag header warning libmamba Could not parse mod/etag header warning libmamba Could not parse mod/etag header warning libmamba Could not parse mod/etag header warning libmamba Could not parse mod/etag header warning libmamba Could not parse mod/etag header pkgs/main/win-64 No change pkgs/main/noarch No change pkgs/r/win-64 No change pkgs/r/noarch No change pkgs/msys2/win-64 No change pkgs/msys2/noarch No change Pinned packages: - python 3.11.* warning libmamba Problem type not implemented SOLVER_RULE_STRICT_REPO_PRIORITY warning libmamba Problem type not implemented SOLVER_RULE_STRICT_REPO_PRIORITY warning libmamba Problem type not implemented SOLVER_RULE_STRICT_REPO_PRIORITY warning libmamba Problem type not implemented SOLVER_RULE_STRICT_REPO_PRIORITY warning libmamba Problem type not implemented SOLVER_RULE_STRICT_REPO_PRIORITY warning libmamba Added empty dependency for problem type SOLVER_RULE_UPDATE Could not solve for environment specs The following packages are incompatible └─ ta-lib is installable with the potential options ├─ ta-lib [0.4.18|0.4.19] would require │ └─ python >=
reference_answer: This should now be resolved since the v0.4.32 PR was merged. Previous Response The ta-lib feedstock appeared to have fallen behind in maintenance. Neither the Python 3.11 nor 3.12 migration PRs had passed at time of the question. Thus, the solver could not install a version of TA-lib in the environment because there was no version available for Python 3.11. Moreover, the Conda solver will not change Python versions (beyond patches) in place without explicitly being told to do so. Instead, create a new environment with Python 3.10 and install it there. conda create -n foo python=3.10 ta-lib Alternatively, one could send a PR to the Conda Forge feedstock to get it updated.
llm_attempt:
The conda-forge ta-lib recipes are pinned tightly to specific Python builds, and your environment's own python=3.11.* pin plus channel priority is causing mamba's solver to find no compatible combination - that's what the SOLVER_RULE_STRICT_REPO_PRIORITY warnings and "incompatible" message mean, not a real absence of a Windows/py3.11 build.

Easiest fix: skip conda for this package. Since TA-Lib 0.4.29+ on PyPI ships prebuilt Windows wheels bundling the compiled C library, just run, inside the activated conda env:

pip install TA-Lib

That avoids the conda/mamba solver and any need to separately compile or install the C ta-lib library. If you specifically need it via conda, try a brand-new environment (mamba create -n taenv -c conda-forge python=3.11 ta-lib) without other pins that could conflict, or drop the python patch-pin so the solver has more room. Also make sure conda-forge is your primary/highest-priority channel, since ta-lib isn't on defaults.

question:
Static verification of type compatibility across Python + YAML + JSON Schema pipeline stage boundaries

Is there an existing tool or pattern that statically verifies type compatibility across pipeline stage boundaries — where stages are defined in Python, configured in YAML, and validated with JSON Schema — before runtime?
llm_attempt:
Not really, as a single tool - the fundamental problem is that Python static type checkers only see Python source; YAML content and JSON Schema documents are opaque to them until parsed at runtime, so nothing can prove cross-boundary compatibility purely statically.

The practical pattern instead is schema-first (or model-first) single-source-of-truth generation: define your stage contracts once, either as JSON Schema and generate Python types from it (e.g. datamodel-code-generator, producing Pydantic models or TypedDicts you can mypy/pyright-check), or as Pydantic/attrs/msgspec models and generate JSON Schema from them (model.model_json_schema() in Pydantic v2). YAML config gets loaded and validated against that same schema/model at load time (Pydantic parsing, or jsonschema.validate), which pushes the actual boundary-compatibility guarantee to "validated immediately at runtime on load" rather than compile-time. Combine that with contract/integration tests per stage boundary. No existing tool gives compile-time proof across Python+YAML+JSON Schema simultaneously; runtime validation at each boundary, generated from one canonical schema, is the accepted substitute.

question:
Problem with DWT3D with Custom Keras Layer

I'm trying to integrate the TFDWT library's DWT3D layer into a custom Keras layer. import tensorflow as tf import keras from TFDWT.DWT3DFB import DWT3D class DWTLayer(keras.layers.Layer): def __init__(self, **kwargs): super().__init__(**kwargs) self.dwt3d = DWT3D(wave='haar') def call(self, x): #x = tf.transpose(x, [0, 2, 3, 1, 4]) return self.dwt3d(x) class SimpleModel(keras.Model): def __init__(self): super().__init__() self.dwt_layer = DWTLayer() self.conv = keras.layers.Conv3D(1, 3, padding='same') def call(self, x): x = self.dwt_layer(x) return self.conv(x) strategy = tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy() with strategy.scope(): model = SimpleModel() model.compile(optimizer='adam', loss='mse') with strategy.scope(): dummy_input = tf.random.normal((4, 128, 128, 128, 4)) try: _ = model(dummy_input, training=False) print("Success") except TypeError as e: print(f" Error: {e}") Error: Error: Exception encountered when calling DWT3D.call(). <tf.Tensor 'dwt3d/concat_2:0' shape=(128, 128) dtype=float32> is out of scope and cannot be used here. Use return values, explicit Python locals or TensorFlow collections to access it. Please see https://www.tensorflow.org/guide/function#all_outputs_of_a_tffunction_must_be_return_values for more information. <tf.Tensor 'dwt3d/concat_2:0' shape=(128, 128) dtype=float32> was defined here: File "<frozen runpy>", line 198, in _run_module_as_main File "<frozen runpy>", line 88, in _run_code File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/colab_kernel_launcher.py", line 37, in <module> File "/usr/local/lib/python3.12/dist-packages/traitlets/config/appl
reference_answer: It failed because there's a conflict between Keras, which automatically inferences shapes, and how TFDWT creates tensors. When you compile the model, Keras tries to determine the shapes of the tensors in the network, so it traces the layer with a scratch graph. It calls self.dwt3d(x) , which triggers dwt3d.build() , which then creates the tensor in that graph. When Keras finishes determining the shapes, it deletes this scratch graph. When the training starts, your DWT3D layer tries to use that matrix, but it can't because it belongs to a graph that was deleted. Your solution will work, but here is a cleaner way to do it: class DWTLayer(keras.layers.Layer): def __init__(self, **kwargs): super().__init__(**kwargs) self.dwt3d = DWT3D(wave='haar') def build(self, input_shape): with tf.init_scope(): self.dwt3d.build(input_shape) super().build(input_shape) def call(self, x): return self.dwt3d(x)
llm_attempt:
That error is TensorFlow's FuncGraph-capture check firing, not a Keras API misuse on your side - it means some tensor is created in one traced tf.function/graph context and referenced from a different one, which is exactly what tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy triggers (each replica gets its own graph). It usually happens when a layer stashes an intermediate tensor as self.something inside call() and reuses it later, instead of only using return values/locals - most likely inside TFDWT's DWT3D implementation itself, not your wrapper.

First isolate it: run the same model/call without strategy.scope() (plain CPU/single GPU). If it works there, the bug is DWT3D's incompatibility with multi-replica graph tracing, not your DWTLayer. Also try tf.config.run_functions_eagerly(True) to confirm it's trace-related. Since this is third-party library code, the real fix likely has to happen inside TFDWT (avoid caching tensors as attributes across calls) - worth checking/filing an issue on the TFDWT repo for MirroredStrategy support, and avoiding MirroredStrategy for this layer meanwhile.

question:
Unable to access oracledb package using python in ODI14c Marketplace

I am facing issue in ODI14c Marketplace, while connecting to Oracle database using Python script. Error is, 'ObjectNotFound'. when i go and see, i can find oracledb package at location python3.8. oracledb package installed Error while accessing oracledb package/library from Python Does anybody face similar issue.
reference_answer: Summary: You are installing OracleDB into one version of Python and then running a different version of Python where OracleDB is not installed. You need to install it into the same Python version as you are running (or vice versa). You run: python3.8 -m pip install oracledb Which shows you that OracleDB is already installed. Then you run: python Which is running Python 3.6.8 , a different version to the version of Python where you installed OracleDB. Instead, either run: python3.8 -m pip install oracledb python3.8 or: python -m pip install oracledb python So that you are installing OracleDB into the environment of the Python version that you are running. Or better, create a Python virtual environment and install OracleDB into that environment and run that: Create the virtual environment once: python3.8 -m venv /path/to/where/you/want/the/venv When you want to use the virtual environment, then activate it: source /path/to/where/you/want/the/venv/bin/activate Note: You should see the command prompt change, indicating that the virtual environment has been activated. Then install OracleDB into the virtual environment (rather than being installed globally) and run the virtual environment's Python: python -m pip install oracledb python
llm_attempt:
This is almost certainly an interpreter mismatch rather than oracledb being truly missing: ODI's embedded Python execution engine (a separate bundled interpreter/runtime, not necessarily the system python3.8 you see on disk) has its own module search path, so pip-installing oracledb into "python3.8" site-packages doesn't make it visible to ODI's Python step unless that's the exact interpreter ODI is configured to use.

Check Topology/Physical Schema (or the Python technology's execution agent settings) for which Python executable/path ODI is actually invoking, and install oracledb into that same environment's site-packages (or point ODI's PYTHONPATH/agent config at the environment where you already installed it). In containerized/Marketplace deployments, also confirm the package persists across container restarts - some Marketplace images reset non-baked-in changes, so ad hoc installs can disappear until baked into the image or installed via a startup script. Without seeing the exact ODI14c Python execution configuration this is a best guess; sharing the "Python execution" agent/path setting from ODI Topology would help pin the fix down further.

question:
Any difference between await asyncio.Task and asyncio.Task.result()?

After the task already completed, is there any difference between await asyncio.Task and asyncio.Task.result() ? The only difference in the following code is how I read the value in task . import asyncio from asyncio import TaskGroup async def func(): await asyncio.sleep(2) return 0 async def main(): async with TaskGroup() as tg: task = tg.create_task(func()) print(await task) asyncio.run(main()) vs import asyncio from asyncio import TaskGroup async def func(): await asyncio.sleep(2) return 0 async def main(): async with TaskGroup() as tg: task = tg.create_task(func()) # The await is implicit when the context manager exits. print(task.result()) asyncio.run(main()) Which code is the preferred one?
reference_answer: The source code snippet below shows that await task ends up calling task.result() if the task is done. So the answer is: no difference in this case. def __await__(self): if not self.done(): self._asyncio_future_blocking = True yield self # This tells Task to wait for completion. if not self.done(): raise RuntimeError("await wasn't used with future") return self.result() # May raise too. # location: asyncio/futures.py, in class _Future, # the Task class is derived from it
llm_attempt:
After the task is done, both give you the same value/exception in this example - but they're not interchangeable in general. task.result() raises asyncio.InvalidStateError if the task hasn't finished yet; it doesn't wait. await task will suspend and wait if the task isn't done, then return the result once it is - so it's safe regardless of task state. If the task raised, both re-raise that exception. If cancelled, both raise CancelledError.

Inside your TaskGroup example specifically, by the time print(await task) runs, or the block exits and you call task.result(), the task is guaranteed complete (either via the explicit await, or because TaskGroup itself waits for all tasks at exit) - so both are safe there.

Prefer await task as the general, idiomatic style since it works whether or not the task has finished yet. Use .result() mainly when you already know completion happened elsewhere, e.g. in a done-callback, or right after a TaskGroup exits, as here.

question:
Using array indices to address another array

I'm trying to "overlay" a numpy 1-d array over another 1-d array of larger size, so that the overlaying array sets multiple values in the overlayed array. I'm struggling with an efficient way to convert the indices from the overlaying array ( overlay ) to the overlayed array ( arr ). overlay = [ 0 , 1 , 1 , 4 , 3] subixs = [[0, 1, 2, 3], [4, 5], [6], [7], [8]] # relationship to `arr`, i.e. overlay[0] sets `arr[0]`, `arr[1]`, `arr[2]` and `arr[3]` assert len(overlay) == len(subixs) arr = [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 4, 3] overlay[1] = 7 should turn arr to [0, 0, 0, 0, 7, 7, 1, 4, 3] because [1] refers to subixs[1] which in turn refers to arr[[4,5]] . This index conversion is easy for scalar indices, but for indices such as boolean arrays it becomes difficult. For instance, imagine: msk = (overlay == 1) | (overlay == 3) overlay[msk] = [44, 48, 47] in that case msk would need to be converted to [4, 5, 6, 8] to be used to the corresponding indices in arr and also the values to be set ( [44, 48, 47] ) would need to be expanded to [44, 44, 48, 47] . I figured out how to do the translation to the indices in arr , but it is rather inefficient as it's using lists and I also haven't figured out how to expand the values. new_value = [44, 48, 47] msk = (overlay == 1) | (overlay == 3) overlay[msk] = new_value # convert to indices in `arr` # Keep as list as numpy requires symmetric arrays subixs = [[0, 1, 2, 3], [4, 5], [6], [7], [8]] subixs = np.asarray(subixs, dtype=object) arr_ixs = sum(subixs[msk], []) new_arr_value = ? # should be `[44, 44, 48, 47]` arr[arr_ixs] = new_arr_value How would I
reference_answer: Your issue is trying to work with lists or object arrays. Numpy is simply not designed for that. Use a flat array instead. # convert subixs to a flat array flat_subixs = np.concatenate(subixs) # compute the lengths once lengths = np.array([len(l) for l in subixs]) arr = np.repeat(overlay, lengths) print(arr) msk = (overlay == 1) | (overlay == 3) arr[flat_subixs[np.repeat(msk, lengths)]] = np.repeat([44, 48, 47], lengths[msk]) print(arr) Output: [0 0 0 0 1 1 1 4 3] [ 0 0 0 0 44 44 48 4 47] This way all the slow computations (concatenation and lengths) are performed only once, and all other operations are vectorized. If you want to mutate overlay this is also possible, just create arr once in the end: msk = (overlay == 1) | (overlay == 3) overlay[msk] = [44, 48, 47] # eventually add other transforms here # finally create "arr" once arr = np.repeat(overlay, lengths) print(arr) # [ 0 0 0 0 44 44 48 4 47]
llm_attempt:
Precompute an "owner" array once: for every position in arr, which overlay index it belongs to. Since subixs partitions arr in increasing, contiguous order, this is just a repeat:

lens = np.array([len(s) for s in subixs])
owner = np.repeat(np.arange(len(overlay)), lens)  # len(owner) == len(arr)

Then both problems collapse into one line each. Boolean-mask assignment:

arr[msk[owner]] = np.repeat(new_value, lens[msk])

msk[owner] fancy-indexes the overlay-space mask into arr-space (owner holds valid indices into msk), giving exactly the arr_ixs mask you derived manually. np.repeat(new_value, lens[msk]) expands each new value by how many arr positions its overlay slot covers, in matching order - for your example this yields [44,44,48,47] at mask positions [4,5,6,8], matching your manual result.

For a plain integer/scalar overlay index i, arr[subixs[i]] = value works directly without needing owner; owner mainly makes the boolean-mask case efficient and vectorized instead of Python-level loops.

question:
Automating Image Classification for Website Content Using Computer Vision

There are a large number of images that need to be uploaded to my organization’s website. Currently, it takes a significant amount of time to manually classify each image into categories such as tower, grass, or concrete. I believe this task can be automated using computer vision techniques, but I am unsure how to begin. I would like to know which computer vision model is suitable for image classification, especially one that is fast and efficient. I have access to a gaming laptop and I am familiar with Python programming, so I am open to implementing a machine learning or deep learning–based solution.
reference_answer: the title does not match the rest of the post ... please correct it
llm_attempt:
For fast, effective classification on a gaming laptop, don't train from scratch - use transfer learning on a small pretrained CNN. MobileNetV2 or EfficientNet-Lite/B0 (via Keras: tf.keras.applications.MobileNetV2(weights='imagenet', include_top=False)) fine-tuned with a new classification head on a few hundred labeled images per category (tower, grass, concrete, ...) trains in minutes on a laptop GPU and runs inference fast, which fits "classify a large batch of images."

To skip labeling for a first pass, try zero-shot classification with CLIP (openai/CLIP or open_clip): embed each image and text prompts like "a photo of a tower", "a photo of grass", "a photo of concrete", and assign the best-matching label - no training required, good enough to bootstrap a labeled dataset or serve as a baseline.

Practical path: label ~200-500 images per category (LabelImg/Roboflow help), fine-tune MobileNetV2 in Keras, evaluate accuracy/confusion matrix, then batch-predict the rest; fall back to CLIP zero-shot if you need something working today.

question:
In Polars, how do you create a group counter / group ID?

How do you get a group_id column like this, grouping by columns col1 and col2 ? col1 col2 group_id A Z 1 A Y 2 A Z 1 B Z 3 based on such a DataFrame : df = pl.DataFrame({ 'col1': ['A', 'A', 'A', 'B'], 'col2': ['Z', 'Y', 'Z', 'Z']} ) In other words, I'm looking for polars equivalent to R data.table .GRP ( df[, group_id:=.GRP, by = .(col1, col2)] ). Thanks ! Context : I want to build an event ID because in my data, I have many detailed rows for one event. Once the event ID is created, I will use it to perform various window operations. I prefer to have this event ID rather than keeping a list of grouping variables.
reference_answer: If you don't care about "first occurrence has lower rank" then you can just rank combination of col1 and col2 columns. pl.struct() to create one column out of col1 , col2 . pl.Expr.rank() to assign rank to rows. df.with_columns(group_id = pl.struct("col1","col2").rank("dense")) shape: (4, 3) ┌──────┬──────┬──────────┐ │ col1 ┆ col2 ┆ group_id │ │ --- ┆ --- ┆ --- │ │ str ┆ str ┆ u32 │ ╞══════╪══════╪══════════╡ │ A ┆ Z ┆ 2 │ │ A ┆ Y ┆ 1 │ │ A ┆ Z ┆ 2 │ │ B ┆ Z ┆ 3 │ └──────┴──────┴──────────┘ Otherwise, it will be a bit more complicated - you can create index to track current row order and then assign rank based on this index. pl.DataFrame.with_row_index() to create an index / row number. pl.Expr.min() and pl.Expr.over() to get minimum index within col , col2 . pl.Expr.rank() to "compress" this minimum to dense rank. ( df.with_row_index("group_id") .with_columns( pl.col.group_id.min().over("col1","col2").rank("dense") ) ) shape: (4, 3) ┌──────────┬──────┬──────┐ │ group_id ┆ col1 ┆ col2 │ │ --- ┆ --- ┆ --- │ │ u32 ┆ str ┆ str │ ╞══════════╪══════╪══════╡ │ 1 ┆ A ┆ Z │ │ 2 ┆ A ┆ Y │ │ 1 ┆ A ┆ Z │ │ 3 ┆ B ┆ Z │ └──────────┴──────┴──────┘
llm_attempt:
For a group id in first-appearance order (matching data.table's default .GRP), build the unique key combinations in the order they first appear, index them, then join back:

groups = (
    df.select(["col1", "col2"])
      .unique(maintain_order=True)
      .with_row_index("group_id", offset=1)
)
df.join(groups, on=["col1", "col2"], how="left")

unique(maintain_order=True) keeps first-seen order rather than sorting, with_row_index (with_row_count on older Polars) assigns 1,2,3,..., and the join broadcasts each group's id back to every matching row - giving group_id = [1,2,1,3] for your example.

If sorted (lexicographic) order is acceptable instead of first-appearance order, a one-liner works: pl.struct(["col1","col2"]).rank("dense") - simpler, but it numbers groups by sorted key order, not by when they first appear, so it won't match .GRP's default ordering exactly.

question:
Service Account Not able to create Google Calendar event with Attendees

I've created a service account on Google Console, and assigned it to Google Cloud Run Service. I think I've got most of it working, if I don't run it with Attendees. If I add attendees, it throws an error. Constraint - The Attendees don't necessarily have to be Domain / Organization Email (user@company.com) but can be any general gmail use (user@gmail.com) Below is the code on Cloud Run SCOPES = ["https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar"] # 1) Get credentials for the service account this service runs as credentials, project_id = google.auth.default(scopes=SCOPES) # Refresh to ensure we have a token and metadata credentials.refresh(Request()) # Get email associated with account sa_email = getattr(credentials, "service_account_email", None) print(f"Authenticated as service account: {sa_email}, project: {project_id}") # 2) Build the Calendar API client service = build("calendar", "v3", credentials=credentials) # 3) Prepare the event event_body = { "summary": summary, "description": description, "start": {"dateTime": start}, "end": {"dateTime": end}, "attendees": [ {"email": test@gmail.com}, {"email": test2@gmail.com}, ], } print("Event Body:", event_body) Error: ERROR: "Service accounts cannot invite attendees without Domain-Wide Delegation of Authority.". Details: "[{'domain': 'calendar', 'reason': 'forbiddenForServiceAccounts', 'message': 'Service accounts cannot invite attendees without Domain-Wide Delegation of Authority.'}]"> What's the right way to setup Domain-Wide Delegation of Authority to get my service-account to create google calendar event without attendees? Woul
llm_attempt:
Domain-Wide Delegation only works if you have a Google Workspace domain - a service account can't invite attendees on its own, and it can't impersonate a plain @gmail.com account either. It has to impersonate a real Workspace user in a domain you administer.

Steps: (1) In Google Cloud Console, enable Domain-Wide Delegation on the service account and note its OAuth Client ID. (2) In Google Workspace Admin Console -> Security -> API Controls -> Domain-wide Delegation, add that Client ID with scope https://www.googleapis.com/auth/calendar. (3) In code, impersonate a real Workspace mailbox:

delegated = credentials.with_subject("realuser@yourworkspacedomain.com")
service = build("calendar", "v3", credentials=delegated)

Create the event via that delegated service; it will be organized by realuser@yourworkspacedomain.com. Attendees can still be any address, including @gmail.com - the restriction is only on who the organizer/sender is, not on recipients. Without a Workspace domain, a service account fundamentally can't send calendar invites; you'd need standard OAuth with a real user's consent instead.

question:
Variadic tuple type parameter

I am trying to annotate a function which receives a tuple of types, and returns a value of one of the provided types. For example: @overload def func[T1](types: tuple[type[T1]]) -> T1: ... @overload def func[T1, T2](types: tuple[type[T1], type[T2]]) -> T1 | T2: ... @overload def func[T1, T2, T3](types: tuple[type[T1], type[T2], type[T3]]) -> T1 | T2 | T3: ... Conceptually analogous to the following invalid code: # invalid def func[*Ts](types: tuple[type[*Ts]]) -> Union[*Ts]: ... Is something like this supported?
reference_answer: Depending on what type checker you use, something like this might work: (playground: Mypy , Pyright , Pyrefly , ty ) # Either def func[T](types: tuple[type[T], ...]) -> T: ... # or def func[T](types: Iterable[type[T]]) -> T: ... reveal_type(f((int,))) # mypy, pyright => int reveal_type(f((int, str))) # mypy => object # pyright => int | str # Pyrefly errors out; ty infers Unknown. This works due to a property of type[] : It distributes over unions . That is, type[A] | type[B] is equivalent to type[A | B] . A type checker might infer the type tuple[type[int], type[str]] for (int, str) and then cast it to tuple[type[int | str], ...] or Iterable[type[int | str]] , which leads to T being resolved as int | str . This behaviour is not guaranteed across type checkers, however, as seen above.
llm_attempt:
This isn't currently expressible with TypeVarTuple. Two separate problems block it: type[*Ts] isn't valid - type[] takes a single type argument, and PEP 646 doesn't define an element-wise "map type[] over each item of Ts" operation, so you can't say "a tuple of type[[each Ts member]]" generically. And Union[*Ts], unpacking a TypeVarTuple directly into Union, isn't part of PEP 646 either - unpacking is only defined for tuple types and *args-like positions, not arbitrary generic aliases like Union, so most checkers (mypy, pyright) reject or don't support it.

In practice, the overload-per-arity style you already wrote (func[T1], func[T1,T2], func[T1,T2,T3], ...) is still the standard, checker-supported way to express this for a bounded number of arities - it's exactly how typeshed handles similarly-shaped variadic builtins. There's no cleaner variadic-generic substitute available today; it would need a future PEP for mapped/distributed tuple types.

reference_answer: there are modules to display tables. They may better format columns and they may add some frame for table. python - Printing Lists as Tabular Data - Stack Overflow

You don't need to sprinkle * characters through the code - build a small helper that pads text to a fixed width using str.center()/ljust() and adds the border characters around it:

WIDTH = 50
def line(text=""):
    print("*" + text.center(WIDTH - 2) + "*")

print("*" * WIDTH)
line(company_name.title())
line(company_address)
line(company_city)
print("*" * WIDTH)

For rows with your tab-based formatting (product name/price), format the inner content first into one string, then wrap it the same way: line("{}  ${}".format(p1_name.title(), p1_price)). Since center() (or ljust/rjust) automatically pads with spaces to WIDTH-2 characters, you write the two border characters once per line, in one place, instead of manually counting/aligning stars around each piece of content - and changing WIDTH later updates every line's border consistently. If you want the fill character itself to be *, pass it as the second argument: text.center(WIDTH-2, '*').

question:
FastAPI, SQLAlchemy Session context

I am working on a project with FastAPI and SQLAlchemy 2.0. According to FastAPI docs, you should pass the Session (from sessionmaker) as Dependency. Something like this: # Dependency def get_db(): db = SessionLocal() try: yield db finally: db.close() It just yields the Session and handles closing (commit, returning to pool). Would this also handle a rollback, if the exception is raised? With SQLAlchemy alone, I would use a context manager, which handles that. But with FastAPI I am not sure. From SA docs: with Session() as session: with session.begin(): [...] And just a note at the end: I am not a fan of using a session per request in the middleware. I use the Session as Dependency now, but I have already encountered some issues: If I use a Session in the dependency, which is used as global (in APIRouter() ) it would use that Session even for the routes, that has their own Session dependency. The issue is, that the Session on APIRouter() is used for something else, then the Session given as a dependency to the endpoint. But as only one Session is used, it mixed up objects in SQLAlchemy identity map and loading strategy. That is just a note not related to the question directly. Thank you.
llm_attempt:
No, not implicitly in the way you'd want: your get_db only guarantees db.close() runs in finally - it never calls commit() or rollback() explicitly. SQLAlchemy's Session.close() does release the current transaction (discarding any unflushed/uncommitted changes) as part of closing, so you won't get a corrupt half-committed state, but you also never get an explicit commit, so nothing persists unless your endpoint code calls db.commit() itself.

The safer, explicit pattern people use with FastAPI mirrors the context-manager idiom you quoted:

def get_db():
    db = SessionLocal()
    try:
        yield db
        db.commit()
    except Exception:
        db.rollback()
        raise
    finally:
        db.close()

This makes the intent (commit on success, rollback on failure, always close) explicit rather than relying on close()'s implicit cleanup semantics. On your router-level note: Depends(get_db) already gives each request its own Session instance - if you saw sessions bleeding across routes, that's likely from instantiating/sharing a Session object directly at import time rather than through Depends.

question:
How should the settings priority system work?

We have three configurations of different levels.: default_settings = {'compression': 'zip'} format_config = {'compression_quality': 85, 'background_color': 'white', 'alpha_channel': 'remove'} base_config = {'compression_quality': 100} And if, for example, write the following code: final_config = {**default_settings, **format_config, **base_config} Then it will work: >>> {'compression': 'zip', 'compression_quality': 100, 'background_color': 'white', alpha_channel': 'remove'} As you can see, "compression_quality" has changed from 85 to 100, since `base_config` has a higher priority and has overwritten this value. BUT other settings remained the same, for example, "compression": "zip" remained, although I did not explicitly specify it in `base_config'. (I understand how this code works, it was given just as an example) Question: do I need to inherit settings from the lower levels, or use ONLY those settings that are explicitly specified in the higher-level configuration?
reference_answer: it is standard behavior for dictionary. It adds and replaces but newer removes. And it is doesn't know what "priority" is. At this moment the only idea is to get base_config.keys() and use it to get values from other dictionares.
llm_attempt:
Cascading/inheriting is the conventional and expected behavior for layered config, and it's what your dict-unpacking code already does correctly - each higher-priority layer should only need to specify the keys it wants to override, with everything else falling through from the lower layers. This matches how essentially every layered config system works (CSS cascades, git config scopes, env vars overriding defaults, argparse defaults): the whole point of a defaults layer is that other layers don't have to repeat it.

Requiring every higher layer to fully respecify all keys defeats that purpose - it's brittle (add a new default key later and every layer needs updating), verbose, and easy to silently drop settings by omission. The only reason to go "explicit-only, no inheritance" is a deliberate isolation/security requirement (e.g. guaranteeing a layer can't unintentionally inherit a stale or sensitive value) - and even then you'd typically implement that as explicit validation/whitelisting per layer, not by abandoning inheritance everywhere.

question:
LibreOffice UNO API: Column Page Breaks Not Resetting, Unlike Row Breaks

LibreOffice UNO API: Column Page Break Issue in Python I'm using the LibreOffice UNO API with Python to programmatically apply row and column page breaks in a Calc spreadsheet. However, I'm facing a discrepancy between how row and column breaks behave. Issue Description When applying row breaks using: rows.getByIndex(row_break_id).IsStartOfNewPage = True ✅ Existing row breaks are correctly reset or overwritten. When applying column breaks using: cols.getByIndex(col_break_id).IsStartOfNewPage = True ⚠ New column breaks are applied, but the initial column breaks in the document are NOT removed. Steps to Reproduce 1️⃣ Starting LibreOffice in Socket Listening Mode I start LibreOffice with the following command: C:\Program Files\LibreOffice\program> start soffice -accept=socket,host=localhost,port=2002;urp; 2️⃣ Connecting to LibreOffice and Accessing the Sheet context = resolver.resolve("uno:socket,host=localhost,port=2002;urp;StarOffice.ComponentContext") desktop = context.ServiceManager.createInstanceWithContext("com.sun.star.frame.Desktop", context) document = desktop.loadComponentFromURL(ods_file_url, "_blank", 0, ()) sheets = document.getSheets() sheet = sheets.getByIndex(0) cols = sheet.getColumns() rows = sheet.getRows() 3️⃣ Attempting to Remove Existing Column Page Breaks Before applying new page breaks, I try to reset all existing column breaks: for i in range(min(cols.getCount(), 100)): # Prevent index error if cols.getCount() < 100 if cols.getByIndex(i).IsStartOfNewPage: print("Page break at column:", i) cols.getByIndex(i).IsStartOfNewPage = False 4️⃣ Verifying If Col
llm_attempt:
Looping over cols.getByIndex(i).IsStartOfNewPage = False to "reset" column breaks is the likely source of the asymmetry - LibreOffice Calc appears to track manual column breaks differently internally than row breaks, and toggling the property per-column doesn't fully clear that internal state the way it does for rows.

Rather than resetting row/column breaks individually, use the sheet-level API meant for this: com.sun.star.sheet.XSheetPageBreak (implemented by the Sheet service) provides removeAllManualPageBreaks(), which clears all manual page breaks - both row and column - in one call:

sheet.removeAllManualPageBreaks()

Call that once before your loop that sets new IsStartOfNewPage = True breaks, instead of looping to reset False first. This sidesteps whatever internal bookkeeping difference causes column breaks to persist, and should give consistent, reproducible behavior matching what you already see for rows. If you specifically need to remove only some breaks rather than all, you'll likely need save/reload of the document between operations, since partial column-break removal via the property setter seems unreliable here.
